In order to avoid skin allergy in the general population, citral should not be present at more than 0.6% in topical preparations. Citral skin sensitization is reduced in some people by the co-presence of d-limonene, but this does not eliminate risk altogether (Robert Tisserand, private communication).
There have been concerns about citral being estrogenic. However, no estrogenic effect takes place in vivo, except possibly in two species of male rat. Citral was not estrogenic in overiectomized mice (34), and in a cancer study, there were no breast tumors in male or female rats fed citral for two years at 0.4% of the diet (35).
There have also been concerns about citral being teratogenic. However, there was no teratogenic effect in rat embryos directly exposed to 200 microM citral (36).
AGP Notes:
The highest concentrations of citral (ranging from 60% to 90%) are found in lemon myrtle, lemongrass, may chang and lemon tea tree oils.

Citral is a mixture of the isomeric compounds geranial (α-citral) and neral (β-citral). They are always found together in essential oils.

Oral citral was analgesic in several rodent assays (3). It has a similar effect to naproxen on inflammatory pain, but unlike naproxen it does not cause gastric injury in rats (2).
The long-lasting inhibition of transient receptor potential channels V1-3 and M8 by citral causes sensory inhibition that may be useful in persistent itch or fibromyalgic types of pain, or allodynia (4).
Oral administration of 100-800 mg/kg of citral in rats was anti-inflammatory in the rat paw edema test (12). At 0.3 mg per ear topically, citral reduced mouse ear edema by 83% (22).
Citral showed an in vitro anti-inflammatory effect (TNF-induced neutrophil adherence) at a concentration of 0.00625% (20).
In two separate reports, Citral was found to inhibit production of the pro-inflammatory substance nitric oxide, with IC50 values of 6.5 and 13.2 microg/mL (21,22).
Citral also suppresses COX-2 expression, though this pathway is less potent than those described above (23).
Citral can reduce inflammation accompanied by edema (24).
Citral has a broad-spectrum antibacterial action, encompassing Gram+ bacteria such as Bacillus subtitlis, Bacillus cereus, Micrococcus spp, Streptococcus agalactiae, Staphylococcus aureus and MRSA, and Gram- bacteria including Escherichia coli, Pseudomonas aeruginosa, Klebsiella pneumoniae, Enterobacter sakazakii and Helicobacter pylori (5,6,7,8,9,10). This activity extends to citral in vapor form (1).
Citral is one of the most potent antifungal essential oil components (17,18) and this extends to citral in vapor form (13,14,15,16,17).
At 0.1 mg/mL, citral was 100% effective in preventing hyphal growth of Trichophyton mentagrophytes, and at 0.2 mg/mL it caused irreversible damage to the fungus (16).
At 200 microg/mL, citral inhibited both hyphal and yeast-form growth of C. albicans (18). Citral showed greater in vitro potency than nystatin against seven Candida strains, including four strains of C. albicans (19).
Citral inhibits the growth of Cryptococcus neoformans, an opportunistic fungus that often causes problems in the last phase of AIDS (17).
Citral is moderately antiviral against HSV-1 in vitro (31).
Citral inhibited contractions in isolated rat uterus suggesting possible use in alleviating menstrual cramps (12).
Citral reduced spasm in isolated rat ileum, with an IC50 value of 20 ng/mL (25).
At 100 mg/kg ip, citral demonstrated moderate sedative and anticonvulsant effects in mice (11,12).
Citral (5% emulsion given i.m.) and citronellal (given orally) together were used to treat 121 cases of advanced carcinoma in Japan. Of these six (5%) were cured, having been followed up for 10-15 years (26).
In in vitro studies, citral inhibited the growth of cells for breast cancer (27), melanoma (28) and leukemia (28,30).
When fed to mice at 1% of their diet, citral prevented the formation of adhesions from abdominal surgery in 60% of animals (33).

Thymol can cause skin or mucous membrane irritation if used at 5% or more, though this is uncommon. At 1% it has never been known to cause any adverse skin reaction (Robert Tisserand, private communication). Best to avoid oils rich in thymol in hot baths.
Thymol inhibits platelet aggregation (33,34). Essential oils high in thymol should therefore be avoided, especially in high or oral doses, before major surgery, and in anyone taking blood-thinning medication, or with blood coagulation issues.
AGP Notes:
Thymol is found in greatest quantity in the thymol chemotype of thyme oil (up to 74%), Monarda citrodora var citriodora (60%) and ajowan (up to 55%).
Thymol is isomeric with carvacrol, and their pharmacological properties are similar. They are invariably found together in essential oils.

The analgesic action of thymol suggests effects in both skeletal and smooth muscle (1,2).
Thymol can act via TRP channel signals and thus modulate mast cell-mediated skin inflammation; it has potential in the treatment of inflammatory skin disorders such as eczema (3).
Thymol has a long-lasting antibacterial action (9), and has shown good efficacy against some antibiotic-resistant strains (6,7). The antimicrobial action of thymol is suggestive of therapeutic effects in infections of the skin, gums, throat, lungs, and GI tract.
Thymol inhibits the growth of Cryptococcus neoformans, an opportunistic fungus that often causes problems in the last phase of AIDS (11).
Thymol was found to have a fungicidal effect on Candida species and a synergistic effect when combined with nystatin (13).
The anti-inflammatory action of thymol involves inhibition of COX-1 and COX-2, and so is similar to medications such as aspirin and ibuprofen. Thymol also inhibits neutrophil chemotaxis (14).
Thymol has antinociceptive activity. possibly via modulating ion channels, receptors and prostaglandin synthesis (16).
Thymol is one of the most potent antioxidant essential oil constituents (17-23).
Experimental evidence suggests antioxidant-related protection that could minimise the side-effects of gamma radiation (19).
Its antioxidant action has been experimentally linked to inhibition of erythrocyte cell death, suggesting possible use in counteracting anemia or the impairment of microcirculation (22).
Thymol has antispasmodic action on the trachea, and it stimulates ciliary activity (25).
Thymol has shown in vitro antitumoral effects in cells for mouse melanoma (26).
Thymol can alleviate cognitive impairments in rodents via anticholinesterase, anti-oxidant and anti-inflammatory actions (28).
Medicines that inhibit acetylcholinesterase are used in cases of cognitive dysfunction, for example people with Alzheimer's disease (31,32).
Thymol is antimicrobial and promotes wound-healing via the stimulation of macrophage migration, and modulation of the growth of fibroblasts and elastase activity (30).

Safety: Internal use of methyl salicylate-rich oils should be avoided in people with gastroesophageal reflux disease. Salicylate are contraindicated in children due to the risk of developing Reye's syndrome. Do not use birch or wintergreen on infants, on damaged skin, or with individuals who are on other salicylate-based medication or warfarin. Topically applied methyl salicylate can potentiate the anticoagulant effects of warfarin, causing side effects such as internal hemorrhage. One teaspoon of the essential oil of wintergreen is equivalent to approximately 7000 mg of salicylate or 21.7 adult aspirin tablets. Ingestion of as little as 4 ml in a child can be fatal. Immediate action should be taken to treat accidental poisoning from birch or wintergreen essential oils. Methyl salicylate in topical analgesic preparations may cause irritation or allergic contact dermatitis and anaphylactic reactions. A considerable amount of salicylic acid may be absorbed through the skin after topical application of methyl salicylate products. This may increase with multiple applications. Caution is advised in clients for whom systemic salicylate may be hazardous or problematic.    Petroleum bases may slightly minimize skin absorption (that's how it's used in BenGay and other deep heat products for muscle aches and pains)

AGP Notes:
Linalol is found in over 200 essential oils. Those with a large percentage of linalol include Ho Wood, Neroli, Bergamot Mint, Coriander, Ghandi root, Rosewood, Basil ct linalol, Thyme ct linalol, Xanthoxylum and Lavender. The form found in coriander seed oil is the d-isomer – it is sometimes called ‘coriandriol’.
Linalyl acetate works synergistically with l-linalol – and that the presence of both is essential for the anxiolytic effect of inhaled lavender oil (47).
Linalol has activity against some bacteria and fungi, but especially so in the presence of other constituents such as α-terpinene, γ-terpinene, limonene, terpinen-4-ol and α-terpineol, suggesting synergistic interactions

All properties below are associated with the l-linalol isomer.
The effects of linalol on pain caused by inflammation and edema are thought to be due to the reduction of nitric oxide synthesis or release, thus preventing its accumulation in tissues. Nitric oxide (NO) contributes to edema, nociception and pain by stimulating the release of cytokines and free radicals, which are pro-inflammatory mediators (7).
Linalol produces marked antinociception against glutamate-induced pain in mice, via a non-opioid central mechanism (18).
Linalol is implicated in the GABA-ergic system, which could explain its anti-convulsive and sedative effects, as well as its analgesic activity (39). It has been suggested that linalol may inhibit glutamate binding, thus acting as a sedative. 
Inhaled linalol has an anxiolytic and relaxing effect in mice, with memory affected only by higher doses (9).
The combination of analgesic, anticonvulsant, hypotensive and sedative actions indicate a CNS depressant action.
Linalol isolated from Lavandula angustifolia was more active against clinical Candida albicans strains than the essential oil, while linalyl acetate was ineffective (16).
An antioxidant effect was seen in the form of inhibiting cerebral lipid peroxidation, which can lead to stroke and other neurological disease.
Linalol enhances oxidative defences. Inhalation of linalol increased antioxidative activity not only in healthy adults but also in Carpal Tunnel Syndrome patients, and reduced blood pressure and pulse rate in CTS patients; linalol may be a useful additional intervention to improve symptoms and quality of life in CTS patients (20).
In vitro antitumoral effects have been reported for human skin, kidney, lymphoma, leukemia and liver cancer cells.
Linalol stimulates interferon-gamma, a cytokine that plays an important role in tumor control, and in immunity against viral and intracellular bacterial infections.
Linalol is active in vitro against herpes viruses 1 and 2, and various adenoviruses (27).
Inhaled linalol repressed stress and changed the gene expression of neutrophils and lymphocytes (33).
Linalol reverses the histopathological hallmarks of Alzheimer’s disease and restores cognitive and emotional functions via an anti-inflammatory effect. Linalool may be an AD prevention candidate for preclinical studies (28).
Linalol improved the activity of anthracyclines against breast cancer cells (45), suggesting that it could complement orthodox drugs by acting in a synergistic manner.

Unlike some monterpenes, β-myrcene is not skin sensitizing, even when oxidized. However, myrcene-rich essential oils should be protected from oxidation, which may lead to polymerization (Robert Tisserand, private communication).
The reproductive toxicity NOAEL (no observed adverse effect level) for β-myrcene is 500 mg/kg in rats (6). This suggests that there is no risk of adverse effects from using essential oils containing β-myrcene during pregnancy.

AGP Notes:
In mice, i.p. doses of β-myrcene ranging from 10 to 40 mg/kg showed analgesic action (2).
It is antinociceptive, acting at central and peripheral sites, perhaps by mediating endogenous opioids and α2-adrenoreceptors β-myrcene has been shown to have a strong analgesic effect on some types of induced pain, but this is dependent on the route of administration. It has been postulated that myrcene causes an increase in cGMP (a regulator of ion channel conductance at the cell surface ), which in turn modulates ion channels (3).
β-myrcene showed an anti-inflammatory action when given orally to mice. This was evidenced by inhibition of nitric oxide, gamma-interferon and interleukin-4 (4).
When administered i.p. to mice at 100 or 200 mg/kg, β-myrcene demonstrated a sedative action, increasing barbiturate sleeping time, inhibiting muscle coordination, and in the open-field test. However, these effects were not significant at 50 mg/kg, suggesting a mild sedative effect (5).

It is found in the 30-60% range in essential oils of hemp, rosemary (β-myrcene ct) and Cape May, and in the 20-30% range in Sitka spruce, West Indian bay, West Indian lemongrass, hop and celery leaf. Mastic and juniper oils contain highly variable amounts of β-myrcene.
